overview: Minoan is the modern name for Bronze Age Cretan culture, with several palatial centers rather than one securely documented island-wide kingdom. Its crafts, exchange networks and administrative writing linked Crete to the wider Mediterranean.

items.text: Palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Mallia and Zakros grouped rooms around central courts. Lighting, ventilation and sanitary facilities formed part of their design.
Cretan hieroglyphic writing and Linear A appear on administrative tablets and ritual objects. Palace record keeping helped organize economic activity.
Wall paintings show rituals and the natural world. Jewelers worked with filigree and granulation, while engravers carved seal stones.
A small agate gem in the Met depicts a griffin and is dated approximately 1450 to 1400 BCE. Objects preserve artistic continuity beyond a single palace destruction.
Crete exported timber, textiles, food and luxury crafts, while importing metals and other raw materials.

Widespread destruction around 1450 BCE accompanied growing Mycenaean influence. Linear B administration and mixed pottery styles followed; neither the destruction nor cultural change has a securely identified single cause.
